children: Bankers in Hong Kong skipped the summer break as an AI-fueled rush for capital sent share sales to a record, defying a bruising selloff in the city's stocks, according to Bloomberg. IPOs, placements and block trades raised $47.5 billion in July-September — the biggest haul ever for the period — pushing this year's total above $92 billion and within reach of the $112.5 billion record set in 2021, though a recent surge in bond yields and poor deal performance are making investors and issuers more cautious. Chinese companies raised ever-larger sums and returned to market faster to fund AI expansion: Alibaba's $10.2 billion follow-on was the biggest deal of the period, Zhongji Innolight raised almost $8 billion in Hong Kong's largest listing in nearly seven years, and AI model maker Z.AI has raised $9.6 billion this year via its IPO, placements and a planned $5 billion stock and convertible-bond sale.

"People raise capital right out of lockup and tend to do so more frequently," said Goldman Sachs' James Wang, head of Asia ex-Japan equity capital markets. "Before, they did it once and it would be quiet for one to two years. Now they do it and three months later they come back. This will continue for a couple of years because of AI. I don't see that pace slowing down." Alongside Z.AI, rival MiniMax and chipmakers Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX and Shanghai Biren returned to market in July soon after their IPO lockups expired. The boom spanned Asia-Pacific, where share sales topped $120 billion in the third quarter, the most for the period in six years; mainland China produced some of the biggest deals, including memory chipmaker CXMT's 66.6 billion yuan ($9.9 billion) IPO, the country's second-largest ever. India also roared back, raising a record $26 billion since July — its best quarter — including a $3.2 billion government selldown in Life Insurance Corp. and the $2.4 billion IPO of National Stock Exchange of India, even as the Nifty 50 Index slumped almost 9.5% from its early-August peak.

The boom has unfolded against a shakier backdrop: the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index slumped as much as 7% in July as investors questioned whether heavy AI spending would pay off, and of Hong Kong's 10 largest deals since July, just two are trading above water, while expectations for further Fed rate hikes tighten financial conditions globally. "Having large transactions trading through the offer price is not helpful for risk appetite," said HSBC's Martin Zoll, adding investors may become "more selective about where they put their money to work" into year-end. Recent Hong Kong listings including Shein and chipmaker Longsys traded down on debut. Still, the pipeline remains substantial — the Philippines' Mynt, owner of GCash, has priced what is set to be the country's largest-ever IPO, and Australia's Firmus Grid is lining up a $5 billion data-center listing. Citigroup's Harish Raman said he expects more IPOs before year-end with international interest "cautiously optimistic," while Wang said that despite more selective investors, "there's still a monster amount of deals coming to the market."

title: AI-Fueled Share Sales Lift Hong Kong Fundraising to a Summer Record
